summary: Adding and subtracting fractions whose denominators are RELATED — one denominator is a multiple of the other (1/3 + 1/6, 3/4 − 1/8, 2/5 + 3/10). The central new idea: when you combine fractions by counting parts, the parts must be the same size, so one fraction is renamed as an equivalent fraction sharing a common unit (common denominator), after which like parts are counted as before. Because the denominators are related, only ONE fraction needs converting (e.g. 1/3 = 2/6), making this a gentle bridge from same-denominator work to fully unlike denominators. Renaming must scale numerator AND denominator together — the heart of getting it right.
misconceptions: Adds across the unlike denominators: 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/9, combining numerators and denominators (NFER's 3/9-type error).
Renames the denominator without scaling the numerator: converts 1/3 to 1/6 and gets 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 — 'just inserts the larger denominator' (IES).
Forgets to simplify the result (leaves 3/6 rather than 1/2), or doesn't recognise the answer can be reduced.

activities.title: Align the strips: cut thirds into sixths to make a common unit
steps: Try to combine 1/3 and 1/6 using a thirds strip and a sixths strip laid together; notice the pieces are different sizes and do not line up as they are.
Cut each third-piece in half so each single third becomes TWO sixth-pieces; watch the label change 1/3 → 2/6 as the one piece splits into two and the numerator ticks 1→2.
Now that every piece is a sixth, combine: 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6.
Simplify 3/6 to 1/2 and check on the strip that 3/6 and 1/2 are the same length.

Repeat the same cut-to-match process for 3/4 − 1/8 (recut quarters into eighths, giving 6/8 − 1/8 = 5/8) and 2/5 + 3/10 (recut fifths into tenths, giving 4/10 + 3/10 = 7/10), simplifying where possible.
activities.insight: When you add by counting parts, thirds and sixths must be made the same size first; cutting each third in two makes it two sixths (so the numerator doubles exactly as the denominator doubles), and only then do both fractions share one common unit and combine by counting like parts.

activities.title: Equivalence-and-combine practice that surfaces common errors
steps: Choose the correct value of 1/3 + 1/6 from options that include the correct answer, 2/9 (the add-across error) and 2/6 (denominator renamed but numerator left at 1).
Match each fraction to its equivalent written over the common denominator (e.g. 1/3 ↔ 2/6, 3/4 ↔ 6/8).
Explain in words why only one of the two fractions needed changing.
activities.insight: Checking equivalence and combining in a scorable format can reveal whether the learner renames both numerator and denominator together and whether they look for a common unit at all; it does not by itself show they can carry out the re-partition unaided.

activities.title: Read a worked conversion, then perform your own
steps: Study a single worked conversion where 1/3 is shown recut as 2/6 over the common denominator, with the numerator and denominator both doubling.
Explain what happened to the top number and why.
Then perform the conversion yourself on a fresh related pair (e.g. rename 2/5 as tenths, giving 4/10) and complete the calculation.
activities.insight: A clear worked example of renaming can anchor the 'scale both parts together' idea, but the learner must then carry out the re-partition themselves to secure it; reading a conversion does not by itself elicit producing one.

checkQuestion: Work these out, showing each step: 1/3 + 1/6, and 3/4 − 1/8. Give each answer in its simplest form.
checkAnswer: 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2. 3/4 − 1/8 = 6/8 − 1/8 = 5/8. Rename one fraction to the common denominator (scaling numerator and denominator together), then combine like parts and simplify.
